summary: A single tin-vacancy (SnV) center in diamond is calibrated as a local on-chip thermometer using temperature-dependent optical transitions ($20$ K to few kelvin) and spin-lattice relaxation time $T_1$ (few kelvin to millikelvin), then applied to characterize microwave- and RF-induced heating in a niobium superconducting coplanar waveguide (CPW) on the same chip. At $2$ GHz and zero field, superconducting breakdown occurs at $P_{	ext{crit}} \approx 17.2$ dBm with abrupt heating to $\sim 7.5$ K (inferred from linewidth), while at $20$ MHz and $400$ mT the CPW shows no measurable heating up to $P_{	ext{RF}} = 9.4$ dBm ($B_{	ext{ac}} \sim 1.2$ mT), establishing a safe operating window for diamond-based quantum nodes.
motivation: Optically addressable spin qubits in diamond are sensitive to local thermal excitations that degrade gate fidelities and coherence times, and superconducting control structures are needed to minimize MW/RF dissipation, but quantifying heating in the same device geometry used for spin control has been lacking.
method: Photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy calibrates the C-transition lineshift and linewidth of SnV-F from $20$ K down to $\sim 1$ K, while off-axis magnetic-field tuning of $T_1$ extends thermometry into the millikelvin regime; this combined thermometer probes local temperature while a niobium CPW on the same membrane is driven at various microwave and RF frequencies under controlled duty cycles.
result: At $2$ GHz the CPW undergoes field-dependent superconducting breakdown ($P_{	ext{crit}} \sim 10$–$17.2$ dBm depending on field orientation) with temperature rise to $\sim 3$–$14$ K; at $20$ MHz and $400$ mT, $T_1$ remains constant within uncertainty up to sharp breakdown at $9.4$ dBm, indicating negligible heating and suitability for long RF pulses in nuclear-spin control.
